feedback: If a learner reports '8.2 coaches' untroubled, ask: 'Can the organiser book two-tenths of a coach? What can they actually order?' Route the quotient back to a bookable whole.

If a learner rounds down to 8 citing '.2 rounds down', ask them to work out 8 × 40 and compare with 328 — surface the 8 people with no seat, then establish that here the context forces rounding UP however small the remainder.
For the 320-people case, affirm that an exact quotient (8) needs no rounding judgement, so the child can see the decision is driven by the leftover, not by habit.
When a learner commits to 9 and justifies it by the stranded people, affirm that they have modelled, not just computed.
For the crates variant, if a learner rounds up by habit, ask what a partly-filled crate means for a FULL-crate count, so they see the direction flips with the situation.
activities.intendedInsight: A computed decimal must be interpreted back against the real question; whether and which way to round is a judgement the context makes, not a rule applied on autopilot. The same arithmetic rounds up for coaches and down for full crates, and when the division is exact (320 ÷ 40 = 8) there is no rounding decision at all.
learnerActions: Take the real job: 328 people need to travel to a match; each coach seats 40. Build a ratio table or double number line, or divide, and land on 8.2.
Make the rounding decision explicitly: do I round? which way? to what accuracy? and WHY — state the reason before trusting the number.
Check the consequence of rounding down: 8 coaches × 40 = 320 seats, leaving 8 people with no seat. Commit to 9 coaches and justify it by those stranded people.
Explain in your own words why the SITUATION (a coach is indivisible, nobody can be left behind) decides the direction, not the nearest-whole rule.
Try the exact-division contrast: if only 320 people travelled, 320 ÷ 40 = 8 exactly, so no rounding decision arises — notice the dilemma only appears when the division leaves a remainder.

Try a variant that rounds the OTHER way: 'how many FULL crates can we pack from 328 apples, 40 to a crate?' — here you round down to 8 full crates (8 apples left over). Explain why the direction differs.
activities.title: Order the coaches: when 8.2 is the wrong answer

feedback: If a learner adds a constant to both quantities on a scale variant, show two rows of a ratio table and ask what you multiply the first row by to reach the second — reassert the multiplicative relationship.
If a learner reaches for a single bar that can't show the rate, ask where the second quantity lives on their diagram, and rebuild with a double number line or ratio table.
Affirm tool choices the learner can justify by the structure of the situation rather than by habit.
activities.intendedInsight: Proportional situations covary multiplicatively; choosing a representation that keeps both quantities in view prevents the common additive error and sets up a correct model before any rounding question arises.
learnerActions: Before computing, pick a tool that matches the structure: double number line or ratio table for ratio/rate, bar model for part-whole ratio and comparison, scale factor for similar shapes.
Set up a ratio/scale problem and keep BOTH covarying quantities visible — e.g. on a double number line label litres against cost, or recipe quantities against servings.
Scale multiplicatively, not additively: check that if one quantity is multiplied by a factor, the other is multiplied by the same factor, rather than adding the same amount to both.
Explain why a single bar that shows only one quantity would hide the rate, and choose a tool that doesn't.
activities.title: Choosing the right tool for a proportional problem

feedback: If a learner reports a cm³ answer in cm or cm², ask whether they measured length, surface, or space filled, and relabel.
If a learner over- or under-states precision, ask what decision the number is for — a tank that must not overflow vs a rough estimate call for different accuracy.
When a learner rounds full-crate counts down and justifies it by the leftover not filling a crate, affirm the context-driven direction.
activities.intendedInsight: Volume is a real capacity, not just a formula output; units must be tracked (cm³ ≠ cm² ≠ cm), and the required precision and rounding direction depend on the physical situation (not overflowing, counting only full containers).
learnerActions: Pack a box or tank with unit cubes to feel volume as capacity, then connect this to the formula V = l×w×h (or V = base area × height).
Compute the volume of a labelled container and keep units alive: distinguish cm (length), cm² (area) and cm³ (volume), and report the answer in the right unit.
Answer a real decision that forces rounding the correct way, e.g. 'how many full crates fit inside?' (round down) or 'will this tank overflow if we pour in X litres?'.

For a measurement like a tank holding 12.7 litres, decide to what accuracy you should state it and say who or what in the situation decides that precision (note: 12.7 is an illustrative figure, not computed from given dimensions).
activities.title: Volume as capacity: pack it, compute it, then decide the accuracy

feedback: If a learner says 'always round up', ask for the full-crates case and let them find that it rounds down, so the rule is replaced by situation-reading.
If a learner offers 8.2 to the client, have the client ask what that means to book, pushing interpretation into whole units.
Affirm answers where the learner names the real consequence (people stranded, a crate left part-empty) as the reason for the direction.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to commit to and justify a context-appropriate rounded answer in dialogue — and to say when 'always round up' fails — shows the judgement is situation-driven, not a memorised rule.
learnerActions: Role-play with an event organiser or engineer who presses for a real decision: 'The maths said 8.2 — do I book 8 or 9? What happens to the other people?'
Commit to a whole, bookable answer and defend the direction of rounding out loud by naming the consequence.
Handle a sprung variant that tests transfer, e.g. 330 people with 44-seat coaches (330 ÷ 44 = 7.5 → 8 coaches), or a round-down full-boxes case, and justify the new decision.
Respond to the challenge 'you always round up in word problems — true?' with a counter-example where rounding up would be wrong.
activities.title: Defend your answer to the client (spoken variant)

feedback: If a learner is fluent on sub-skills but stalls on the modelling decision, direct them to the ordering/crates/tank tasks where the computed number must be interpreted.
Note that a correct bare quotient (e.g. 8.2) can be 'right' as arithmetic yet wrong as the real answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency with the component operations supports, but does not replace, the modelling judgement; a correct computation is only the start of answering the real question.
learnerActions: Practise isolated sub-skills on short items: compute a volume from a labelled diagram, simplify a ratio, or complete a row of a ratio table.
Immediately feed each checked sub-skill back into a full modelling task that requires the rounding-in-context decision, rather than stopping at the computed number.
activities.title: Sub-skill checks feeding the real task
